overview: Error handling in Python uses the try/except/else/finally construct to catch and respond to runtime exceptions instead of letting them crash the program.
Exceptions are objects that propagate up the call stack until caught; catching specific exception types (not bare except) keeps error handling precise and prevents masking bugs.

Robust handling combines raising and re-raising, custom exception classes, exception chaining with 'raise ... from', context managers for guaranteed cleanup, and retry logic - all essential for resilient data pipelines.
learningObjectives: Master the full try/except/else/finally control flow and understand exactly when each block executes.
Learn to catch specific exceptions, define custom exception hierarchies, chain exceptions with 'from', and apply EAFP vs LBYL.
Apply context managers and retry patterns to build fault-tolerant data pipelines that fail cleanly and recover from transient errors.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: An exception is an event raised during program execution that disrupts the normal flow of instructions. Python represents exceptions as instances of classes derived from BaseException; the try statement defines a block where exceptions can be caught and handled by matching except clauses, with optional else (runs if no exception) and finally (always runs) blocks for control and cleanup.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Think of try/except like a safety net under a tightrope walker. The 'try' block is the risky walk; if the walker falls (an error occurs), the 'except' net catches them so the show goes on instead of ending in disaster. 'finally' is the cleanup crew that sweeps the stage whether the walker fell or not.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Structured exception handling entered mainstream languages in the 1970s-80s (e.g., CLU, Ada). Python adopted try/except from its inception in 1991. The 'else' clause and context managers (PEP 343, the 'with' statement, Python 2.5) refined cleanup semantics, and exception chaining via 'raise ... from' (PEP 3134) arrived in Python 3 to preserve the original cause of errors.

whyItMatters.business: Unhandled exceptions cause pipeline failures, data loss, and missed SLAs. Graceful error handling keeps dashboards fresh, prevents corrupted reports, and avoids costly 3 AM incident pages.
whyItMatters.engineering: Precise exception handling separates recoverable conditions (retryable network blips) from fatal bugs, making code easier to debug and maintain. Custom exceptions give callers a clear contract for failure modes.
whyItMatters.scalability: In distributed pipelines processing millions of records, a single bad row should not kill the whole job. Targeted handling and dead-letter routing let processing continue at scale.
whyItMatters.cost: Retries with backoff avoid wasteful full-job reruns, and clean failures prevent expensive partial writes that require manual cleanup. Catching too broadly hides bugs that later cost far more to fix.
whyItMatters.reliability: finally blocks and context managers guarantee resources (connections, file handles, locks) are released even on failure, preventing leaks and deadlocks that erode system reliability over time.

coreComponents.name: try block
coreComponents.definition: The block of code that may raise an exception and is monitored for errors.
coreComponents.purpose: To isolate risky operations so failures can be intercepted rather than crashing the program.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Contains only the minimal code that can fail; should be kept narrow so the except clause targets the right operation.

coreComponents.name: except clause(s)
coreComponents.definition: One or more handlers that match specific exception types and run when a matching exception is raised in the try block.
coreComponents.purpose: To handle, log, transform, or recover from a known failure mode.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Catch specific types, optionally bind the instance with 'as e', avoid swallowing errors silently, and re-raise when recovery is impossible.

coreComponents.name: else and finally blocks
coreComponents.definition: else runs only if the try block completed without raising; finally runs unconditionally after try/except/else.
coreComponents.purpose: else holds the success path (keeping it out of try); finally guarantees cleanup of resources regardless of outcome.
coreComponents.responsibilities: else: success-only logic. finally: release files, connections, locks; never swallow exceptions by returning from finally.

internalWorking: When code raises an exception, Python creates an exception object and begins unwinding the call stack, looking for an enclosing try whose except clause type matches (via isinstance, so subclasses match their base).

The first matching except clause runs; if none matches in the current frame, the exception propagates to the caller's frame, continuing up until caught or until it reaches the top level and terminates the program with a traceback.

Regardless of whether an exception was raised or caught, any finally block on the path runs during unwinding; if a new exception is raised inside except, Python records the prior one as __context__ (implicit chaining) or __cause__ (explicit 'raise ... from').
coreConcept.architectureFlow: try (risky op) -> [exception raised?] -> yes: match except clause -> handle/re-raise ; no: run else -> always: run finally -> continue or propagate
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A pipeline calls load_record(row) inside a try block while iterating a large batch.
2. The function raises ValueError on a malformed row; Python searches the active except clauses.
3. The 'except ValueError as e' clause matches, logs the bad row, and routes it to a dead-letter queue instead of crashing.
4. The loop continues to the next row; the finally block flushes the metrics counter regardless of success or failure.

keyTerminology.meaning: The process by which an uncaught exception travels up the call stack frame by frame until a matching handler is found.
keyTerminology.importance: Understanding propagation explains why handlers can be placed far from where the error originates and why bare excepts mask bugs.

keyTerminology.meaning: Linking a new exception to the original cause via __cause__ ('raise X from Y') or __context__ (implicit during handling).
keyTerminology.importance: Preserves the root cause in the traceback, which is critical for debugging layered pipeline failures.

keyTerminology.meaning: EAFP ('Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission') uses try/except; LBYL ('Look Before You Leap') checks conditions first with if statements.
keyTerminology.importance: EAFP is the idiomatic Python approach and avoids race conditions; knowing both helps choose the right style per situation.

importantConcepts.explanation: Catch the narrowest exception type that you can actually handle. A bare 'except:' or 'except Exception:' catches everything - including KeyboardInterrupt (only with bare except), typos, and programming bugs - masking real problems. Always prefer 'except SpecificError:'.

Subclass Exception (not BaseException) to create domain-specific errors like PipelineConfigError. They make failure modes explicit, allow callers to catch precisely, and can carry structured context (e.g., the offending record ID).

Use a bare 'raise' to re-raise the current exception unchanged (preserving the traceback). Use 'raise NewError(...) from original' to wrap a low-level error in a higher-level one while keeping the original cause visible.

variationsAndTypes: **Built-in exceptions:** ValueError, KeyError, TypeError, FileNotFoundError, ConnectionError, TimeoutError - a rich hierarchy rooted at BaseException.
**Custom exceptions:** User-defined classes inheriting from Exception, often grouped under a base like PipelineError for catch-all-domain handling.
**Exception groups (Python 3.11+):** ExceptionGroup and 'except*' allow raising and handling multiple concurrent exceptions, useful with asyncio task groups in parallel pipelines.
advantages: **Separation of concerns:** Keeps error-handling logic distinct from the main happy-path code, improving readability.
**Graceful degradation:** Lets programs recover from or isolate failures instead of crashing entirely.
**Guaranteed cleanup:** finally and context managers ensure resources are always released.
**Rich diagnostics:** Tracebacks and exception chaining preserve the full story of what went wrong.
disadvantages: **Overuse hides bugs:** Catching too broadly (bare except) can silently swallow programming errors.
**Performance on hot paths:** Raising and catching exceptions has overhead; using exceptions for ordinary control flow in tight loops can be slow.
**Complexity creep:** Deeply nested try blocks become hard to read and reason about.
**Resource leaks if misused:** Forgetting finally or context managers can leave connections and files open after an error.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use exceptions for genuinely exceptional conditions and recoverable failures (I/O errors, network timeouts, invalid external data), and use EAFP when the 'check then act' would create a race condition.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid using exceptions for expected, high-frequency control flow in performance-critical loops, and avoid broad catches that obscure logic errors; prefer explicit conditionals (LBYL) when a cheap, race-free check exists.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Exception handling is like a hospital triage system. A specific 'except' clause is a specialist who only treats a known condition; a bare except is a doctor who tries to treat everything and ends up misdiagnosing. The 'finally' block is the discharge process that always cleans the room, whether the patient recovered or not. Exception chaining is the medical chart that records the original injury even after later complications.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Catching Exception (or bare except) is a safe way to make code robust.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Broad catches mask bugs like typos and logic errors, swallow KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit (with bare except), and make failures invisible. Robustness comes from catching specific, expected exceptions and letting unexpected ones surface.

commonMisconceptions.myth: finally cannot run if the try block returns or raises.
commonMisconceptions.reality: finally always runs - after a return, break, continue, or exception - which is exactly why it's used for cleanup. The only exceptions are os._exit() or a hard process kill.

productionConsiderations.scalability: At scale, handle per-record errors locally (log + dead-letter) so one bad row doesn't fail an entire batch; reserve job-level failure for systemic problems like a down database.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Combine retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient errors, idempotent operations, and context managers for cleanup to keep pipelines reliable across flaky networks and services.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Use try/finally or context managers to guarantee resource release on failure, and design partial-failure handling (checkpointing, dead-letter queues) so jobs can resume rather than restart from scratch.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Emit structured logs and metrics on exceptions (type, count, record id) and alert on error-rate spikes; never silently pass, which hides degradation.
productionConsiderations.security: Never expose raw tracebacks or exception messages containing secrets to end users or logs that leave the trust boundary; sanitize error details and log full context only internally.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Targeted retries and dead-lettering avoid full-job reruns, and narrow try blocks reduce wasted compute on operations that were going to fail anyway.
productionConsiderations.performance: Keep try blocks small, avoid exceptions as control flow in hot loops, and prefer EAFP only where the failure is genuinely rare; for high-frequency expected conditions, a cheap conditional check is faster.

codeExamples.title: Full try/except/else/finally with specific exceptions
codeExamples.overview: Demonstrates the complete control flow, catching specific exceptions, using else for the success path, and finally for guaranteed cleanup when reading a config file.
codeExamples.code:
import json
import logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

def load_config(path: str) -> dict:
    f = None
    try:
        f = open(path, "r")
        data = json.load(f)
    except FileNotFoundError as e:
        log.error("Config file missing: %s", path)
        raise
    except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
        log.error("Invalid JSON in %s: %s", path, e)
        raise
    else:
        # Runs only if no exception occurred
        log.info("Loaded %d config keys", len(data))
        return data
    finally:
        # Always runs - cleanup
        if f is not None:
            f.close()
codeExamples.breakdown: The try block opens and parses the file. Two specific except clauses handle a missing file and malformed JSON separately, each logging and re-raising. The else block runs only on success, keeping the happy path out of try. The finally block closes the file handle whether or not an error occurred.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: On success: logs 'Loaded N config keys' and returns the dict. On a missing file: logs the error and re-raises FileNotFoundError. In all cases the file handle is closed.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Putting the return inside finally would swallow exceptions. Catching the broad 'except Exception' here would hide unexpected bugs like a typo in 'json.load'.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Prefer the 'with open(path) as f:' context manager instead of manual finally - it closes the file automatically and is more concise (shown in the next example).

codeExamples.title: Custom exceptions, chaining, and a retry decorator
codeExamples.overview: Shows a custom exception hierarchy, wrapping a low-level error with 'raise ... from', and a reusable retry-with-backoff decorator for transient pipeline failures.
codeExamples.breakdown: PipelineError is a base custom exception; SourceUnavailableError subclasses it so callers can catch either. The retry decorator retries only the specified transient exceptions with exponential backoff, and on final failure raises SourceUnavailableError 'from last' to preserve the original ConnectionError as __cause__ in the traceback.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: fetch_batch retries 3 times with increasing delays (0.5s, 1.0s), then raises SourceUnavailableError whose traceback shows 'The above exception was the direct cause' pointing to the ConnectionError.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Catching a broad Exception in the retry would also retry non-transient bugs. Forgetting 'from last' loses the original cause. Missing functools.wraps loses the wrapped function's name and docstring.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Add random jitter to the backoff to avoid thundering-herd retries, and cap the maximum delay. Make the retried operation idempotent so a partially completed retry does not duplicate data.

codeExamples.title: Context manager for cleanup and EAFP vs LBYL
codeExamples.overview: Implements a context manager for a database connection (guaranteed cleanup) and contrasts EAFP versus LBYL for safely accessing a dictionary key.
codeExamples.breakdown: The @contextmanager decorator turns a generator into a context manager: code before yield acquires the resource, the with-body runs where yield is, and the finally guarantees conn.close() runs on normal exit or exception. The EAFP version attempts the access and handles KeyError; the LBYL version checks membership first.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: The connection is closed even if conn.execute raises. Both get_region functions return 'us-east' for {'region': 'us-east'} and 'unknown' for an empty dict.
codeExamples.commonIssues: In multithreaded code, LBYL's check-then-act can have a race (key removed between check and access); EAFP avoids this. Forgetting the try/finally in the context manager leaks the connection on errors.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use dict.get('region', 'unknown') for the single-key case - it's cleaner than both. Use the class-based __enter__/__exit__ protocol when you need more control or to suppress exceptions.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A nightly ETL job ingests JSON event files from an unreliable S3-like source into a warehouse. The source occasionally times out, some files contain malformed records, and the job must not crash on a single bad file or row - it must retry transient failures, quarantine bad records, and always release connections.
endToEndExample.inputData: Hundreds of JSON Lines files per night, each with thousands of event records; a fraction of records have missing required fields or invalid types, and the object store intermittently returns connection timeouts.
endToEndExample.architecture: A Python ingestion service uses a retry decorator for source reads, a custom PipelineError hierarchy, per-record try/except with a dead-letter sink, and a context-managed warehouse connection. Metrics and structured logs feed a monitoring dashboard.
processingSteps: 1. Open a context-managed warehouse connection so it is guaranteed to close.
2. For each file, call fetch_file wrapped in the retry decorator to handle transient ConnectionError/TimeoutError with exponential backoff.
3. Parse each line in a try block; on json.JSONDecodeError or a custom ValidationError, log the record and write it to a dead-letter queue, then continue.
4. On a valid record, insert it into the warehouse inside the else path.
5. In finally, flush metrics (records_ok, records_failed) regardless of outcome.
endToEndExample.output: Valid records loaded into the warehouse, malformed records routed to a dead-letter store with the original error attached, and a per-run summary of success/failure counts.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Structured logs tag each error with file name, line number, and exception type; metrics track failure rate per file and retry counts, with alerts firing if the dead-letter rate exceeds a threshold or retries exhaust repeatedly.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Transient source errors are retried; permanent per-record errors are quarantined without failing the job; only systemic failures (warehouse unreachable, repeated source exhaustion raising SourceUnavailableError) abort the run, with the original cause preserved via exception chaining.
endToEndExample.finalResult: The pipeline completes nightly even when individual files or rows fail, achieves high data completeness, isolates bad data for later inspection, and never leaks connections - turning a brittle script into a fault-tolerant service.

industryUseCases.problem: Event ingestion pipelines receive billions of events; some are malformed or arrive during downstream outages, and a single failure must not stop the stream.
industryUseCases.solution: Per-event try/except routes bad events to dead-letter topics, custom exceptions classify failure types, and retries with backoff handle transient sink unavailability.
industryUseCases.benefits: Continuous ingestion, no data loss (quarantined for reprocessing), and clear visibility into error categories for debugging.

industryUseCases.problem: Payment processing must distinguish recoverable network errors from fatal validation errors, and must never leave a transaction in a half-committed state.
industryUseCases.solution: Specific exception types per failure mode, idempotent retries for transient gateway timeouts, and context managers / try-finally to guarantee transaction rollback on failure.
industryUseCases.benefits: Correct financial state, automatic recovery from transient failures, and auditable error chains via exception chaining.

industryUseCases.company: Cloud Data Warehousing (e.g., Snowflake, Databricks customers)
industryUseCases.problem: Large batch ETL jobs reading from many external APIs frequently hit rate limits, timeouts, and occasional schema drift in source data.
industryUseCases.solution: Retry decorators with exponential backoff and jitter for rate limits, custom SchemaError for drift detection, and dead-letter handling so jobs complete with partial success.
industryUseCases.benefits: Jobs complete reliably within SLA windows, avoid expensive full reruns, and surface schema problems early through typed exceptions.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Handle errors at the smallest granularity that makes sense (per record or per partition) so failures stay localized; use dead-letter queues and checkpointing so large jobs degrade gracefully rather than failing wholesale.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Combine idempotent operations, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and guaranteed cleanup via context managers so the system recovers from transient faults and never leaks resources during partial failures.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Design handlers to fail over to replicas or alternate endpoints on ConnectionError, and ensure retries respect circuit breakers so a hard-down dependency does not amplify load and reduce overall availability.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Persist progress (offsets, checkpoints) inside finally/cleanup paths so that after a crash the job resumes from the last good point rather than reprocessing everything; keep dead-letter data durable for replay.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Keep try blocks narrow, avoid exceptions for high-frequency expected conditions (use conditionals there), and pre-validate cheaply when it removes a hot-path raise/catch cost.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Targeted retries and dead-lettering avoid full-job reruns; capping retry counts and using backoff prevents runaway compute spend against a failing dependency.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Sanitize exception messages before logging or surfacing them - tracebacks can leak connection strings, tokens, or PII; log full detail only to secured internal sinks and return generic messages to external callers.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Emit structured, machine-parseable error events (exception type, code, record id, retry count) and build dashboards on error rate, retry exhaustion, and dead-letter volume to detect regressions quickly.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Use custom validation exceptions to enforce schema and value constraints at ingestion; quarantine failures rather than silently dropping or coercing them, preserving the original cause for analysis.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log at appropriate levels (warning for handled/retried, error for re-raised, critical for job abort), include exception chains, and alert on error-rate spikes and repeated retry exhaustion rather than on every single handled error.

recommendedPractices: **Catch the narrowest exception you can handle:** prefer 'except FileNotFoundError' over 'except Exception' over bare 'except:'.
**Use try/except/else/finally correctly:** keep the happy path in else and cleanup in finally so try stays minimal.
**Chain exceptions:** wrap low-level errors with 'raise HighLevelError(...) from original' to preserve the root cause.
**Use context managers ('with') for resources:** they guarantee cleanup more reliably and concisely than manual try/finally.
engineeringStandards: Never use a bare 'except:' in production code; if you must catch broadly, use 'except Exception' and re-raise after logging.
Define a project-wide custom exception base class so all domain errors share a common ancestor for catch-all handling.
Always log or handle caught exceptions - silent 'except: pass' is forbidden except for explicitly documented, narrow cases.
designRecommendations: Distinguish transient (retryable) from permanent (non-retryable) errors via distinct exception types.
Make retried and re-run operations idempotent so partial failures do not duplicate or corrupt data.
Route per-record failures to a dead-letter sink instead of aborting an entire batch.
namingConventions: Suffix custom exception classes with 'Error' (e.g., PipelineConfigError, SchemaValidationError).
Group related exceptions under a descriptive base class (e.g., PipelineError) named after the domain.
Name the bound exception variable 'e' or 'exc' consistently (e.g., 'except ValueError as exc').
documentationStandards: Document which exceptions each public function can raise in its docstring (a 'Raises:' section).
Document the retry policy (count, backoff, which exceptions) for any function that retries.
Document dead-letter behavior and how to reprocess quarantined records.
testingStrategies: Write tests asserting that the correct exception type is raised for invalid input (pytest.raises).
Test that finally/cleanup runs on both success and failure paths (e.g., mock a connection and assert close was called).
Test retry logic with a mock that fails N times then succeeds, asserting the call count and backoff behavior.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using a bare 'except:' or broad 'except Exception:' that swallows everything.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers want to 'make the error go away' or avoid crashes during development without thinking about which errors are actually recoverable.
commonMistakes.impact: Masks bugs (typos, logic errors), catches KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit (bare except), and produces silent failures that are extremely hard to debug.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Catch only specific, expected exceptions you can handle; let everything else propagate. If catching broadly for logging, re-raise afterward.

commonMistakes.mistake: Losing the original cause when wrapping exceptions.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Catching a low-level error and raising a new one without 'from', so the traceback shows only the new exception.
commonMistakes.impact: Debugging becomes much harder because the root cause is hidden; on-call engineers see a generic wrapper error with no clue about what actually failed.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use 'raise NewError(...) from original' to chain, or re-raise unchanged with a bare 'raise' to preserve the original traceback.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting a return or break inside a finally block.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Misunderstanding that finally runs last, so a return there seems convenient for cleanup-then-return.
commonMistakes.impact: A return/break/continue in finally swallows any in-flight exception and overrides return values, silently hiding errors.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use finally only for cleanup side effects (closing resources); never return or alter control flow from it.

comparisonSection.explanation: Specific except handles only known, recoverable failures and lets bugs surface, making code robust and debuggable. Bare except catches everything including programming errors and (for bare except) KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit, masking problems and producing silent, hard-to-trace failures.

EAFP is idiomatic Python, race-free (no gap between check and use), and reads cleanly when failures are rare. LBYL can be clearer and faster when the check is cheap and the failure is common, but it risks TOCTOU race conditions in concurrent code and can become verbose with many conditions.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between the else and finally blocks in a try statement?
beginnerQuestions.answer: The else block runs only if the try block completes without raising an exception, and is used for the success path. The finally block runs unconditionally - after success, after a handled or unhandled exception, and even after a return - and is used for cleanup like closing files or connections.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Interviewers want to confirm you know else is success-only while finally is always-run. Mention that keeping the happy path in else keeps the try block minimal.

beginnerQuestions.question: Why is a bare 'except:' considered bad practice?
beginnerQuestions.answer: A bare except catches every exception, including KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, and also masks programming bugs like typos or wrong attribute access. This produces silent failures that are hard to debug. You should catch specific exception types you can actually handle.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Emphasize that 'except Exception' is slightly better (it excludes KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit) but still too broad for most cases. The principle is: catch only what you can handle.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is exception chaining and how do you control it?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Exception chaining links a new exception to its cause. Implicit chaining happens automatically when an exception is raised inside an except block (stored in __context__). Explicit chaining with 'raise NewError(...) from original' sets __cause__ and shows 'direct cause' in the traceback. Using 'raise NewError(...) from None' suppresses the chain.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: This tests understanding of __cause__ vs __context__. Stress that chaining preserves the root cause, which is vital for debugging layered systems.

intermediateQuestions.question: Explain EAFP vs LBYL and when you'd use each.
intermediateQuestions.answer: EAFP (Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission) tries the operation and catches exceptions; it's idiomatic Python and avoids race conditions. LBYL (Look Before You Leap) checks preconditions with if statements first. Use EAFP when failures are rare or a check would create a TOCTOU race; use LBYL when the check is cheap, failure is common, and concurrency isn't a concern.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A strong answer mentions the race-condition advantage of EAFP (e.g., file existence can change between check and open) and the readability/perf trade-offs.

intermediateQuestions.question: How would you implement retry logic for a flaky network call?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Wrap the call in a loop that catches only transient exceptions (ConnectionError, TimeoutError), sleeps with exponential backoff plus jitter between attempts, and re-raises after a maximum number of attempts - ideally wrapping the final failure in a domain exception via 'from'. The operation should be idempotent so retries are safe.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Look for: catching specific transient errors only, capped retries, backoff with jitter, idempotency, and preserving the cause. A decorator implementation shows extra maturity.

advancedQuestions.question: What is the difference between __context__ and __cause__, and how does 'raise from None' behave?
advancedQuestions.answer: __context__ is set implicitly whenever a new exception is raised while handling another, recording the previous exception. __cause__ is set explicitly by 'raise X from Y' and indicates a deliberate causal link, printed as 'direct cause'. 'raise X from None' sets __suppress_context__ so neither the context nor cause is displayed, giving a clean traceback when the original is irrelevant.
advancedQuestions.explanation: This probes deep knowledge of Python 3's chaining model. Mention that suppressing context is useful when wrapping internal errors you don't want to leak.

advancedQuestions.question: How do ExceptionGroup and 'except*' (Python 3.11+) change error handling in concurrent code?
advancedQuestions.answer: ExceptionGroup bundles multiple exceptions raised concurrently (e.g., by an asyncio TaskGroup) into one object. The 'except*' syntax matches and handles a subset of the group by type, splitting it so each handler gets only the matching exceptions while the rest propagate. This lets you handle several independent failures from parallel tasks without losing any.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Relevant for modern async pipelines. Show you understand that pre-3.11 only one exception could surface from concurrent failures, losing information.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your batch ETL job crashes whenever a single record in a million-row file is malformed. How do you make it resilient without ignoring data quality issues?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Identify granularity: the failure should be per-record, not per-job. Decide what 'resilient' means: continue processing, but don't silently drop bad data. Choose to catch the specific parse/validation exceptions, quarantine the bad record with its error, emit metrics, and continue. Reserve job-level failure for systemic problems.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Wrap per-record processing in a try/except that catches specific validation/parse exceptions, write the offending record plus the original error to a dead-letter store, increment a failure metric, and continue the loop. Only abort the whole job for systemic errors (e.g., warehouse unreachable). This preserves resilience and data-quality visibility.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design the error-handling strategy for a service that ingests data from dozens of third-party APIs with varying reliability and writes to a central warehouse.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Define a custom exception hierarchy (base PipelineError, with TransientError and PermanentError subclasses). Wrap each API call with a retry decorator that retries only TransientError with exponential backoff and jitter and a circuit breaker. Use context managers for warehouse connections. Route PermanentError (schema/validation) records to a dead-letter store. Emit structured error events and metrics.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Retries improve resilience but add latency and risk amplifying load on a failing dependency (mitigated by circuit breakers and capped attempts). Dead-lettering preserves data at the cost of needing a reprocessing path. Broad catches simplify code but hide bugs, so handling stays type-specific.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Process records in parallel partitions with per-partition error isolation; use ExceptionGroup/except* for concurrent task failures. Persist checkpoints in cleanup paths so the job resumes after crashes. Scale dead-letter storage independently and provide a separate replay job to reprocess quarantined records.

How does 'raise' with no arguments differ from 'raise e' inside an except block?
Why should custom exceptions inherit from Exception rather than BaseException?
How would you test that a context manager releases its resource when the with-body raises?
When is it appropriate to catch 'except Exception' rather than a specific type?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Exception handling uses try/except/else/finally to catch, classify, recover from, and clean up after runtime errors instead of crashing.
keyConcepts: try/except/else/finally: risky code, handlers, success-only, always-run cleanup.
Specific over bare except: catch only what you can handle.
Chaining: 'raise X from Y' (__cause__) vs implicit __context__.
EAFP vs LBYL: try/except idiom vs check-first.
commands: raise CustomError("msg") from original  # explicit chaining
with open(path) as f: data = f.read()  # auto cleanup
interviewPoints: else runs only on success; finally always runs (even on return).
Bare except catches KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and masks bugs.
Use 'from' to preserve the root cause in tracebacks.
EAFP avoids TOCTOU race conditions that LBYL can introduce.
Retry only transient exceptions, with backoff, jitter, and idempotency.
quickNotes: Custom exceptions should subclass Exception and share a domain base class.
Never put return/break/continue in finally - it swallows exceptions.
Don't use 'except: pass' - silent failures hide degradation.
Context managers (with) are preferred over manual try/finally for resources.
Route per-record failures to a dead-letter queue; reserve job abort for systemic errors.

keyTakeaways: try/except/else/finally gives precise control: try holds risky code, except handles specific errors, else runs only on success, and finally always runs for cleanup.
Catch the narrowest exception you can actually handle - bare and overly broad excepts mask bugs and produce silent, hard-to-debug failures.
Preserve the root cause with exception chaining ('raise X from Y') and use bare 'raise' to re-raise unchanged, keeping tracebacks meaningful.
Build resilient pipelines with custom exception hierarchies, retries (backoff + jitter + idempotency) for transient errors, and dead-letter routing for permanent ones.
Use context managers ('with') to guarantee resource cleanup, and prefer EAFP over LBYL to write idiomatic, race-free Python.
